newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada says airdrops probably not needed in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Canada says airdrops probably not needed in Zaire.

text.p: The international coalition trying to deliver aid to eastern Zaire probably will not have to make food airdrops or intervene militarily in any major way, Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young said on Thursday.

"It doesn't look as though they (airdrops) are going to be required in any significant way because the NGOs (non-governmental organisations) are in that area on the border between Zaire and Rwanda," Young told reporters.

"I think all of us around the world are going to have to focus on how we provide humanitarian aid but I don't think at this stage it will require any major military intervention," he said after the Cabinet considered the Zaire situation.

Canada began assembling international support four weeks ago for a 10,000-strong military force to move into eastern Zaire to help what aid agencies said were more than a million refugees or displaced people receive aid or go home to Rwanda.

That was scaled down a week ago, at least for the time being, to a headquarters force in Uganda that would continue to investigate refugee needs and prepare for airdrops if necessary -- which now looked increasingly less likely.

Young and Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said aid agencies had been allowed to deliver some aid into areas of eastern Zaire where they had previously been restricted. And they said an agreement between Tanzania and Rwanda for the return of half a million refugees to Rwanda would now make aid to Rwanda even more important.
Some aid workers in the field question whether the refugees in Tanzania will want to go home. But Young declared: "It is very clear that the goal now will be humanitarian aid, especially in Rwanda."

Nearly 600,000 Rwandan refugees in Zaire have returned home and many others have become scattered close to Rwanda or are Hutu refugees fleeing deeper into Zaire in the face of advances by Tutsi rebels. Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 when minority Tutsis took control of the country after a massacre of around a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.

"If you take the original numbers (in Zaire), which were in excess of a million, we're now looking at numbers scattered throughout that area perhaps more on the order of 100,000 (or) 200,000," Young said. "And many of these people are either displaced Zairians or Rwandans who have no desire to return to Rwanda for obvious reasons."
He added: "We're not identifying massive aid needs at this point. I mean, there are some people who have some medical needs, there's no question, but by and large it's going very well."

Young said later that Canadian soldiers on a special disaster response team that had been waiting on 24-hour standby at Trenton, Ontario, had been taken off standby. This does not affect the 300 Canadian troops in Uganda and Rwanda.
International Cooperation Minister Don Boudria said he would help lead a December 13-14 multipartite mission to the Rwandan capital to support the reintegration of refugees.

This will follow up a Nov. 23 meeting of donors he chaired in Geneva. Its objective will be to agree on a plan to re-establish the refugees who have come home as well as the 500,000 he said were expected to return from Tanzania.

Asked if the multinational force might be disbanded, Axworthy said: "We're continuing to hold meetings with our partners ... We assess it as it goes along." He added that he would have further discussions in Europe next week but said no meetings were planned for the weekend.
